records.notes: FR-040 boundary class: tearing down a workspace that has no container. Removal of nothing is the degenerate end of the operation and must succeed — a `down` that failed here would be unusable as a cleanup step, which is how it is actually used.

Covers the high-risk triple `hrt-down-compose-running-cli-overlay`. Teardown identifies what to remove from the Compose project name and the workspace labels, both derived from the resolved configuration; a command-line overlay re-enters that derivation. If it does not reproduce what `up` used, `down` reports success and leaves the project running — which is why success is not the assertion: the following exec into the service container has to fail.

SC-004 requires every operation to carry a case for each configuration source the applicability rules permit for it. Teardown of a container built from a Dockerfile. The container is removed; the IMAGE the build produced is deliberately not asserted on, because `down` removes containers and leaving a built image behind is the correct half of 'what it removes and what it leaves' (FR-039).

FR-040 malformed class: `down` derives the resources to remove FROM the configuration, so an unparseable document leaves it with nothing it can trust. Failing is the honest outcome; succeeding would claim a teardown that could not have been scoped. This diverged on the 024 live run and was FIXED in deacon rather than characterized: `down` was falling through to auto-discovery on a parse error, which re-derives the identity from a DEFAULT configuration — so a `down` over an unreadable document silently scoped the teardown differently from the `up` that created the container, then exited 0 having removed nothing. `up` and `exec` already rejected the same document; `down` was the one subcommand that did not.

FR-039 teardown: after `down --remove` the workspace's container is GONE, which a `down` exit code cannot show — a teardown that removed nothing exits 0 too. The third operation execs into the container that should no longer exist and must fail; that failure is the evidence. (The container-graph channel cannot serve here: it reads an inspect the runner captures at an `up`/`exec` boundary, and after a successful removal there is nothing left to inspect.) The pinned reference has no `down` command, so this is evaluated against the declared expectation. This diverged on the 024 live run — `op-verify` still succeeded, i.e. the container was NOT removed — and was FIXED in deacon rather than characterized. Root cause was not `down` at all: the host-global state index is a read-modify-write over a shared file, and with four cases running concurrently in `docker-shared` each process republished the whole in-memory map, silently erasing the entries the others had written. `down` then found no state for its workspace and removed nothing while exiting 0. The read-modify-write is now serialized under an advisory lock (crates/core/src/cache/disk.rs); `--remove --all` was never affected because it is label-driven rather than index-driven.

FR-040 unsupported class: a workspace folder with no devcontainer configuration at all. The request is well-formed and the folder exists; the configuration simply cannot be provided. CORRECTED after the 024 live run. The case previously declared `expectFailurePhase: config-resolution` and a non-zero exit, and diverged — that expectation described a contract deacon has never held. The class is right; the OUTCOME column of the class table ('rejects, later') is a typical consequence, not a definition, and for an idempotent teardown the unsupported input is ACCEPTED. That is the fact worth recording here: `down` treats "nothing to tear down" as a successful outcome, exactly as in case-down-boundary-no-container and case-errorpath-down-repeat-teardown, and its auto-discovery path still resolves a container recorded for the workspace PATH — so teardown genuinely survives the configuration being deleted rather than failing to scope. Nine integration tests in crates/deacon/tests/integration_down.rs already pin exit 0 here. The input `down` does reject is an UNREADABLE document, which case-down-malformed-config-rejected covers and deacon now rejects: absent means nothing to scope, unparseable means the scope cannot be trusted.

Error-path tier, teardown stage: `down --remove --all` against a workspace whose resources were ALREADY removed by the preceding teardown. Every operation runs past configuration read, and the input is one both implementations accept — the tier's premise. The second teardown is the case's subject: `down` derives what to remove from labels and the resolved configuration, and encountering a container that is no longer there is an error path it must absorb, because `down` is used as a cleanup step whose whole value is that it can be run when the state is unknown. The failure the case records is the exec's: a `down` exit code cannot distinguish a teardown that removed something from one that removed nothing, so removal is evidenced by a command targeting the container that must no longer exist. The failing operation is that exec rather than `down` itself because the closed failure-phase set (022 data-model §8) names no teardown phase — see `phases_reachable_by`. Spec-expectation because the pinned reference has no `down` command at all.

`--all` is deliberate and load-bearing. Plain `down --remove` resolves the container through the host-global workspace-state index under `$TMPDIR/deacon-state/`, which is written atomically but READ-MODIFY-WRITTEN without a lock: two concurrent `deacon up` runs clobber each other's entries, and the loser's `down` then finds no state, logs "No running containers or compose projects found for workspace" and exits 0 having removed nothing. Reproduced 3 runs in 4 at concurrency 4 (024 US4). `--all` takes the LABEL-driven path instead — 6 of 6 under the same load — and is also the identification the reference and the VS Code extension use, so it is the more spec-faithful teardown to pin. The state-index defect is deacon's to fix and is not characterized away here; it is reported as a runtime bug, and the pre-existing `case-down-*` cases that still use plain `down --remove` remain intermittent because of it.
